catalog_quote: [p.93] Because each word has its own stress, there are actually three stressed syllables in each of these pause groups. However, one syllable in each pause group (/ka/, /a/ and /ti/) has an additional stress. ... 3. STRESS GROUP (PHONOLOGICAL WORD) A stress group consists of a group of 1-3 syllables, but 4-6 syllable stress groups occur frequently in verbs. Stress occurs on the last high tone or on the first syllable if there are [no] highs. 3.1 One-Syllable One-syllable stress groups carry stress with both high and low tone. ... [p.94] 3.2 Multi-Syllable Two-syllable stress groups carry stress on the last high tone, or on the first syllable if there are no highs. (H-H) ... (H-L) ... (L-H) ... (L-L) ... Three-syllable stress groups follow the same pattern as two-syllable, with the last high tone syllable receiving stress, or the first syllable if there are no highs. There are no recorde…

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Martin 1991 text we hold at pp. 92-94 and 98 exactly as the locator says. (2) Martin 1991 is a first-hand 30-pp. SIL phonology and the only phonological description of Sikaritai that exists per Glottolog 5.1 (2 descriptive refs total; full sources.bib scan shows only ethnographic, wordlist and comparative items otherwise). (3) Two open comparative works were downloaded to Clouse 1997 (PL A-85) p.152 confirms two tonemes and calls Martin's system pitch accent, p.160 says stress is non-contrastive across Lakes Plain — confirming the tonal coding with tone-determined word prominence ('last H, else initial'); Clouse & Clouse 1993 (LLM 24) is segmental and silent. sources.citation: Clouse, Duane A. 1997. Toward a reconstruction and reclassification of the Lakes Plain languages of Irian Jaya. In Karl Franklin (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 2, 133-236. Pacific Linguistics A-85. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: p.152: 'All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent.' p.160: 'stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date.'
sources.locator: sec. 11 'Tone typology' p.152; Appendix 3 intro p.160

sources.citation: Clouse, Heljä & Duane Clouse. 1993. Kirikiri and the Western Lakes Plain languages: selected phonological phenomena. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 24(1): 1-18.
sources.quote: Segmental phenomena only (stops, fricativisation, nasals, vowels, syllable closure; Sikaritai data from Martin 1991). No statement on Sikaritai stress or tone; conclusion defers 'syllable structure and tone' to future research.

sources.note: A phonological sketch of Sikaritai written 16 years after Martin 1991 and cited in a tone-typology article (Yoder 2018) — expected to contain a tone/suprasegmental section (Martin 1991 reports 2 tonemes H/L plus tone-conditioned stress); actual content not seen.
